source.description: WoRTool map catalog, full-map images, map marks, and the Both-sides order of battle.
source.map_image_note: 66 maps are the PNG produced by the map viewer's download control (1994x1994, with base/objective/battery marks and labels). Six maps have no marked-download asset in WoRTool; their original map images are included instead. Picket Patrol has 12 source images.

10lb-parrott-rifle.name: 10Pdr. Parrott Rifle
10lb-parrott-rifle.description: Unlike the 3-inch Ordnance Rifle's reputation, the Parrott had tendencies to burst when firing due to the gun being made from cast iron, unlike the wrought iron structure of the 3-inch, leading to a lower popularity. During the Maryland Campaign, an estimated 69 guns were in Union service, with 50 in Confederate service. Over 500 Parrott rifles, along with related variants, were produced during the war and used by both sides.

12lb-m1857-napoleon.name: 12Pdr. Napoleon M1857
12lb-m1857-napoleon.description: The most popular cannon during the war, with over 1,500 guns having been produced. 131 Napoleons were used by the Union, and an estimated 30 were used by the Confederates during the Maryland Campaign. It was the most common artillery piece used by both sides during Antietam, with 117 of the total 131 being used during the battle by Union batteries, and 14 of 30 being used by Confederate batteries.

12lb-m1861-napoleon.name: 12Pdr. Napoleon M1861
12lb-m1861-napoleon.description: The most popular cannon during the war, with over 1,500 guns having been produced. 131 Napoleons were used by the Union, and an estimated 30 were used by the Confederates during the Maryland Campaign. It was the most common artillery piece used by both sides during Antietam, with 117 of the total 131 being used during the battle by Union batteries, and 14 of 30 being used by Confederate batteries. This variation was produced by Confederate armories, and was distinguished by the lack of a flared muzzle.

3-inch-m1861-ordnance-rifle.name: 3-inch Ordnance Rifle M1861
3-inch-m1861-ordnance-rifle.description: The most common rifled artillery model used during the Maryland Campaign, and second most common model used during the Civil War. Its popularity came from the reliability and accuracy of the guns, made from wrought iron. Confederate versions were of lower quality, leading to more problems and lower popularity in the Confederate Army. The guns were of such high quality that there is only 1 reported bursting of the gun during the war, when a Pennsylvania battery loaded double canister during the Battle of the Wilderness. There were an estimated 83 guns used by the Union, and 49 used by Confederate batteries during the Maryland Campaign. The gun remained the main rifled artillery piece of the US Army until 1879-81 when the remaining guns were modernized.

bloater.name: Bloater
bloater.description: These unsightly freaks are bloated and disfigured, distinguished by their pale green glow. However, their cumbersome look is most deceptive, as they can quickly approach their victims among crowds of sprinters. Be sure to keep them beyond arms reach, or you and your compatriots will encounter an early, explosive end.

brute.name: Brute
brute.description: This ungodly abomination towers over anything in its vicinity, seeking nothing but destruction. Its cry can raise the dead from their slumber, summoning runners to aid in its assault. When at range, it will tear up the ground where it stands and throw a boulder at any stationary man or fortification, punishing the careless with a quick and brutal death. The only ways to stop this lumbering beast in its tracks are by unleashing volleys or bombardments.

cheval-de-frise.name: Cheval de Frise
cheval-de-frise.description: Rows of sharpened stakes, driven into stout frames, now line your defenses. Any of the undead foolish enough to stumble against them will find their advance met with splinters.

gabions.name: Gabions
gabions.description: Woven wicker baskets, filled with earth and stone, now stand ready to blunt the charge of the shambling masses. A humble barrier, but one that may mean the difference between life and an early grave.

inferno-titan.name: Inferno Titan
inferno-titan.description: "May God have mercy on us all."

palisade-wall.name: Palisade Wall
palisade-wall.description: Hewn logs, set firm into the ground, rise high against the press of the horde. Tall and unyielding, a wall to hold the line when all else falters.

sprinter.name: Sprinter
sprinter.description: These ghouls are more reckless than their brethren, aggressively sprinting to any fortification and group it seeks to tear down. Any soldier caught defenseless by a sprinter is sure to join the unending ranks of the risen.

torch.name: Torch
torch.description: Surrounded and overwhelmed by mindless undead, regimental colors no longer serve a purpose in what little remains of the military. What were once Color Bearers now find themselves armed with a lit torch, serving as bright rally points that lead the way through hell.

walker.name: Walker
walker.description: The restless dead have risen from the ground, seeking blood and bone. Friend and foe alike have banded together to contain the new threat, and to ensure that the innocent may flee from their ceaseless wrath.

colt-army-m1860.name: Colt Army M1860
colt-army-m1860.description: A revolver produced by Colt that uses the same frame as the M1851 Navy, is chambered in .44 caliber, weighed 2lbs, and had a length of 14in. With 200,00 of these produced and around 127,000 sold to the US government, this was the most widely used sidearm in the Civil War, primarily by the United States Army. The revolver was produced with a small cylinder to make use of a silver spring steel, with controlled carbon content with improvements to strength. The thinner cylinder made in manufacture sometimes caused the revolver to explode when fired.

lemat-m1855.name: LeMat M1855
lemat-m1855.description: This entire revolver is a mix of unusual parts fitted to make a gun, from its 9-round capacity cylinder, to the 20-gauge secondary barrel it revolves around, capable of firing buckshot. The LeMat went through multiple prototypes, ranging from .40 caliber, 20 gauge to .36 caliber, 28 gauge, before finally being produced in .36" or .44" with 20 gauge. Only 2,500 of these revolvers were produced along multiple other variants, being shipped through the Union blockade of the South. The LeMat revolver was made in many variants: Muzzleloading, Pinfire, Centerfire, Carbine, and the Baby LeMat at the rarest, being a shortened version with only 100 produced. In War of Rights, Press "5" to toggle ammo types.

lorenz-m1854.name: Lorenz M1854
lorenz-m1854.description: A rifle originally developed by a Lieutenant in the Austrian Army. It sported the modern percussion cap system and had three main variants produced: a full-length rifle issued to marksman units, a shortened service rifle, and a carbine, becoming the most popular variant. About 325,00 of these rifles were sold to the Union and Confederacy throughout the war. The Union version was known to be rebored to .58 caliber to use standardized ammunition, while the Confederacy retained the .54 caliber for the war.

mississippi-m1841.name: Mississippi M1841
mississippi-m1841.description: Originally produced in a smaller .54 caliber instead of .58" or .69". The rifle got its name from its use by the Mississippi Riflemen during the Mexican-American war. Later in the war, the rifle was rebored to use the more common .58 caliber instead of the original .54". The number of rifles produced is unknown, but the weapons factory at Harper's Ferry and private contractors are known to have produced at least 70,000.

pattern-enfield-m1853.name: Pattern Enfield M1853
pattern-enfield-m1853.description: Being the standard issue rifle of the Confederacy, hundreds of thousands of these rifles were smuggled past the Union blockade to aid the confederates. Chambered in .58 and changeable to a .577 caliber Minié ball. Estimates of rifle purchases are around 500,000 by the Union, with unknown numbers bought by the Confederacy. The M1853 sports a 55in barrel length and weighed 9lbs.

sharps-carbine-m1859.name: Sharps Carbine M1859
sharps-carbine-m1859.description: The Sharps carbine was the preferred firearm for mounted troops due to its shorter length and lighter weight compared to the full-length rifle. Like the rifle variant, it used a breech-loading mechanism that made reloading on horseback far easier than with muzzle-loading weapons. The carbine was chambered for the same paper cartridge system, giving cavalry units a significant advantage in rate of fire.

sharps-rifle-m1859.name: Sharps Infantry Rifle M1859
sharps-rifle-m1859.description: The Sharps Rifle was issued to sharpshooter and cavalry units on both sides of the war. The M1859 featured a breech-loading system that allowed for faster loading than any rifle from its era. There were two variants of the Sharps produced: A full-lenght variant for infantry, and a Carbine variant for cavalry. The full-length guns had 11,000 produced, although most never saw use during the war. The carbine variant had almost 90,000 produced, most of which being supplied to cavalry units.

scoped-sharps-rifle.name: Sharps Rifle M1859 Scoped
scoped-sharps-rifle.description: This variant of the Sharps Rifle is equipped with a 6x magnification scope. In War of Rights, Press "Z" to switch sights.

springfield-m1842.name: Springfield M1842
springfield-m1842.description: The M1842 was produced in the standard .69 caliber for muskets. Many of these muskets were converted M1840's that had their flintlock mechanisms replaced with the new percussion cap system. Originally being produced with smoothbore barrels, these models proved to be inaccurate and would later have rifling be added to allow for the use of the new Minié ball. The M1842 spouted a total length of 58in and a weight of 10lbs, with a total of 275,000 muskets being manufactured. In War of Rights, press "5" to toggle ammo types.

springfield-m1855.name: Springfield M1855
springfield-m1855.description: A standard issue percussion rifle at the start of the war. Around 60,000 were produced by the start of the war before thousands were destroyed when the Confederates captured Harper's Ferry, with thousands more being used by the Confederacy. The M1855 had a length of 58in, weighed 9lbs, and was chambered in .58 caliber instead of the previous .69 caliber as it was found to be more accurate when firing a Minié ball.

springfield-m1861.name: Springfield M1861
springfield-m1861.description: One of the first rifles to feature standardized sights, as they were previously wielded onto the gun following production. By the end of the war, almost 1 million of these guns and their variants were produced as a result of their increasing demand. Produced with a barrel length of 56in and a relatively low weight of 9.5 lbs, and chambered in .58 caliber.

whitworth-rifle-m1854.name: Whitworth Rifle M1854
whitworth-rifle-m1854.description: The Whitworth had a very unique .45 hexagonal caliber, along with a hexagonal-shaped bore to fit the bullet. Some of the rifles were made with the 4x Davidson telescopic sight mounted along the left side of the barrel. The Whitworth was considered the first true sniper rifle, being able to accurately hit a target at distances greater than 1,000 yards. The Whitworth was so accurate that it was responsible for the death of Major General John Sedgwick, who was sniped by Confederate sharpshooters from around 1,000 yards. Sedgwick was quoted saying, "They couldn’t hit an elephant at that distance." before he was instantly shot under the left eye, killing him instantly. He was the third highest ranking officer in the Union Army at the time he died, behind Maj. General Meade and Lt. General Grant.

scoped-whitworth.name: Whitworth Rifle M1854 Scoped
scoped-whitworth.description: This variant of the Whitworth Rifle is equipped with a 4x magnification scope. In War of Rights, Press "Z" to switch sights.

us-foot-officer-sword-m1850.name: US Foot Officer Sword M1850
us-foot-officer-sword-m1850.description: The most popular style and model of sword used by the army was worn by Majors and below from 1851 to 1865. This sword also replaced the US Marine Corps' standard sword from 1859 to 1875. It had an overall length of 38" (31" blade length), and weighed 3.5lbs.

us-light-cavalry-saber-m1860.name: US Light Cavalry Saber M1860
us-light-cavalry-saber-m1860.description: This cavalry saber was designed during a time when cavalry in the US was being reformed, culminating in their official designation as a branch of the United States Army in 1861. More than 300,000 of these sabers were produced in the Civil War with an overall length of 41" (35" blade length), and replaced the cumbersome M1840 Heavy Cavalry Saber as a significantly lighter alternative. However, their usage on both sides waned along with cavalry charges, as skirmishing and reconnaissance overtook their primary role. As a result, cavalrymen gradually replaced most of their swords with carbines and revolvers by 1865.

maps.name: Alexander Farm
maps.description: From 1860 to 1861, a surge of over one hundred thousand enthusiastic Southern men enlisted in the Confederate army. Their motivations for volunteering varied, encompassing both a naive thirst for adventure and susceptibility to peer influence.

maps.name: Anderson's Counterattack
maps.description: September 14th - 18:00 Fox's Gap: With but a few hours of daylight left the 9th and 89th New York along with Clark's Battery take up a defensive position on the northern side of Fox's Gap, defended by Garland's, now broken, Brigade earlier in the day. CSA Gen. G.B. Anderson, arriving with badly needed reinforcements to the remnants of the Confederate force, targets Clark's Battery and the two New York regiments for his counterattack.

maps.name: Bloody Lane
maps.description: September 17th - 09:00: A sunken road often used by farmers becomes a natural fort against a Union onslaught of Rebel lines as Union General French pushes forward with his 3rd Division and becomes engaged with elements of Confederate General D.H. Hill's Division entrenched in the road.

maps.name: Bolivar Heights Camp
maps.description: September 15th - 09:00: The Bolivar Heights was an important and strategic position for Union forces during their garrison of the town, the ridge also serving as a partial campsite to the 15,000 stationed in the beautiful valley. In this fictitious scenario, Confederate forces have breached the hastily-made defences, while Union forces desperately try to muster a counterattack.

maps.name: Bolivar Heights Redoubt
maps.description: September 15th - 10:00: The Bolivar Heights was an important and strategic position for Union forces during their garrison of the town, the ridge also serving as a partial campsite to the 15,000 stationed in the beautiful valley. In this fictitious scenario, Confederate forces are attacking the artillery redoubt of the entrenched Union forces.

maps.name: Burnside Bridge
maps.description: September 17th - 11:30: After several hours of preparation, Union General Burnside is ready to advance the IX Corps against Confederate General Toombs' Brigade of skirmishers whom, while being vastly outnumbered, holds the heights overlooking the Lower Bridge crossing Antietam Creek.

maps.name: Colquitt's Defence
maps.description: September 14th - 19:00 Turner's Gap: Positioned behind a stonewall at the base of Turner's Gap and on the fenced-in Dahlgren Road running above the gap, overlooking the National Road headed into Turner's Gap, CSA Colonel Colquitt's brigade readies itself for the attack it knows is coming after having witnessed Union Gen. Hatch's attack on Garnett to the left of Colquitt's brigade an hour earlier. On the National Road in front of them, Union Gen. Gibbon's brigade begins its slow but steady push with an iron-like determination.

maps.name: Confederate Encampment
maps.description: The sheer scale of over a million casualties is incomprehensible. The Civil War's tragedy is perhaps most poignantly captured in the blood-soaked letters of dying soldiers and the tear-stained correspondences of their grieving loved ones.

maps.name: Cooke's Countercharge
maps.description: September 17th - 12:00: After several hours with no reinforcements, Union General Greene is forced to withdraw from his salient in the West Woods. Confederate Colonel Cooke orders a countercharge towards Mumma Farm in response to the fleeing Federals.

maps.name: Corn Crib
maps.description: Conquest map in the Drill Camp campaign.

maps.name: Cox's Push
maps.description: September 14th - 11:00 Fox's Gap: As the 30th and 12th Ohio attack the left flank of Garland's Brigade, Union Division Commander Jacob Cox pushes forward the 36th and 23rd Ohio to engage the Confederate 5th North Carolina as well as the 23rd North Carolina, having just reinforced the stretched out and besieged Confederate line. Between the two lines is Fox's Gap, a windswept, valley-like gap covered in stonewalls, fencing in the numerous fields covering the area.

maps.name: Crecy's Cornfield
maps.description: A significant portion of the soldier's service was spent in camp under the supervision of officers, some of whom were strict disciplinarians. Therefore, a substantial portion of the soldier's time was allocated to mitigating the monotony.

maps.name: Crossley Creek
maps.description: To be a member of the vaunted colorguard or the bearer itself was considered a great honor and a source of unit pride to be the color company. But bearing the colors came at the cost of being the most dangerous position in the line.

maps.name: Crossroads
maps.description: When Abraham Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers to put down the rebellion, loyal men of the Union flocked to recruiting stations. Most enlisted out of a sense of duty, to uphold the union founded by the nation's forefathers.

maps.name: Downtown
maps.description: September 15th - 10:00: In this fictitious scenario, the Confederates have breached Camp Hill, and are now assaulting the downtown area of Harper's Ferry where the last defenders doggedly try to hold out against them.

maps.name: Drill Camp CSA
maps.description: Drill Camp map in the Drill Camp campaign.

maps.name: Drill Camp USA
maps.description: Drill Camp map in the Drill Camp campaign.

maps.name: Dunker Church
maps.description: September 17th - 10:30: Union General Greene pushes his Division towards the rebel-held whitewashed church on the outskirts of the West Woods from the direction of the burning Mumma Farm. The church is a focal point of several Union attacks as it sits elevated on a small plateau.

maps.name: East Woods
maps.description: September 17th - 07:20: As Confederate General Hood attempts to push the advancing Union General Hooker's I Corps back into the Cornfield, some of his forces also push against the Union holding in the East Woods directly adjacent to Miller's Cornfield.

maps.name: East Woods Skirmish
maps.description: September 16th - 20:00: During the late afternoon of September 16th, General Hooker takes his Corps across Antietam creek at the upper bridge in order to locate the rebel flank. In the waning light, the 42nd PA and 3rd PA reserves are sent out in a skirmish formation to probe the East Woods for rebels.

maps.name: Farmland
maps.description: Conquest map in the Antietam campaign.

maps.name: Flemming's Meadow
maps.description: The soldier’s diet depended on more than just hardtack and coffee; but not much more. Whether cooked by their comrades or by a designated cook, food except for special occasions was usually a spartan affair that left the soldier pining for the comforts of home.

maps.name: Forest Stream
maps.description: Conquest map in the Antietam campaign.

maps.name: Framing Fencelines
maps.description: Conquest map in the Antietam campaign.

maps.name: Garland's Stand
maps.description: September 14th - 10:00, close to Fox's Gap: CSA Brig. General Samuel Garland having been ordered by Maj. Gen. D.H. Hill to defend Fox's Gap and its road - directly exposing the wagon trains of the Confederate army should it fall, is now deploying his brigade next to the Wise Farm. To his immediate front Union Colonel Scammon's brigade consisting of the 30th and 12th Ohio is advancing and engaging with the 13th and 20th North Carolina while the 23rd Ohio is putting pressure on his far too drawn-out line's right flank.

maps.name: Hagerstown Turnpike
maps.description: September 17th - 06:30: Upon leaving Miller's Cornfield, the Union attacks the Confederates who are defending the Hagerstown Turnpike, a road running next to the cornfield. Its fenced in sides and the road itself functions as a clear line between Jackson's forces in the West Woods and Hooker's south of the cornfield.

maps.name: Harpers Graveyard
maps.description: September 15th - 14:30: In this fictitious scenario, following the taking of Bolivar Heights, the Confederates are launching an assault on the last holdouts of the garrison via the historic Harper's Graveyard.

maps.name: Hatch's Attack
maps.description: September 14th - 18:30, close to Turner's Gap: In an effort to secure the southern part of South Mountain itself and thus open up the flank of Confederate Major General D.H. Hill situated at the strong defensive positions at Mountain House and on the Dahlgren Road at Turner's Gap, Union Brig. Gen. John Hatch's 3500-man division pushes onwards and upwards through some of the most difficult and rocky terrain of the battlefield. On top of the crest CSA General Garnett's 400-man division is rushing forwards to safeguard the flank of the mountain.

maps.name: High Street
maps.description: September 15th - 11:00: In this fictitious scenario, the Union garrison under General Miles attempt to defend the north side of Camp Hill against Confederate assaults after their taking of the Bolivar Heights.

maps.name: Hill's Counterattack
maps.description: September 17th - 17:00: Confederate General Hill arrives from Harper's Ferry late in the day with his Light Division partially wearing captured Federal uniforms. The Division smashes into the flank of the advancing Burnside's Corps which has been delayed heavily earlier in the day at the Lower Bridge.

maps.name: Hilltop
maps.description: Conquest map in the South Mountain campaign.

maps.name: Hooker's Push
maps.description: September 17th - 06:00: In the early fog of dawn, Union General Joseph Hooker pushes southwards with his I Corps, starting from the edge of North Woods, past the R. Miller Farm and through the Miller Cornfield only to be engaged south of it by defending Confederate General Ewell's Division at about 7 AM.

maps.name: Larsen Homestead
maps.description: The unprofessional conduct of volunteer officers and enlisted men, even in the execution of basic linear tactics, dismayed their professional superiors. Costly combat experiences served as an unforgiving instructor as volunteers painfully learned to become professional soldiers.

maps.name: Limestone Bridge
maps.description: Conquest map in the Antietam campaign.

maps.name: Log Cabin
maps.description: Conquest map in the South Mountain campaign.

maps.name: Maryland Heights
maps.description: September 13th - 09:30: Early on the morning of the 13th, Kershaw's and Barksdale's Brigades of Confederates attack the Maryland Heights while the 32nd Ohio and 126th New York try to guard the approach to Harper's Ferry.

maps.name: Miller's Cornfield
maps.description: September 17th - 07:00: An hour after the early morning actions of General Hooker and his Corps near the Miller farmstead, the damaged cornfield is subjected to a new infusion of blood, this time from the men of Hood's division. A withering fire from several sides mean that terrible casualties are wrought.

maps.name: Nicodemus Hill
maps.description: September 17th - 08:45: Confederates are defending Jackson's artillery positioned on Nicodemus Hill from the Union attacking from the direction of Miller farm. The commanding viewpoint offered by Nicodemus Hill offers Washington's, Chew's, and Pelham's batteries devastating fire down the Union lines.

maps.name: Orchards
maps.description: Conquest map in the Drill Camp campaign.

maps.name: Otto & Sherrick Farm
maps.description: September 17th - 12:30: The idyllic farms of the Otto and Sherrick families becomes a heavily contested area as the two forces clash. The farms are situated in close proximity to the Lower Bridge and moving towards the town of Sharpsburg dictates passing their grounds.

maps.name: Outskirts
maps.description: Conquest map in the Harpers Ferry campaign.

maps.name: Overlook
maps.description: Conquest map in the Harpers Ferry campaign.

maps.name: Pat's Turnpike
maps.description: Although often characterised as unprincipled and unlettered individuals with limited intellectual curiosity, soldiers frequently engaged in the political discourses of their day and had a voracious appetite for reading, especially of newspapers.

maps.name: Picket Patrol
maps.description: Picket Patrol map.

maps.name: Piper Farm
maps.description: September 17th - 16:30: The 7th Maine is ordered by Colonel Irwin to push past the bodies at the Bloody Lane, the Piper Cornfield, the apple orchard and attack the Piper farm buildings themselves, which act as headquarters for Confederate Wing Commander General Longstreet. 4 Confederate brigades await them.

maps.name: Pry Ford
maps.description: September 17th - 09:30: In this alternate scenario, grey-clad soldiers hold an important point near a ford on the Antietam Creek, and are attacked by dismounted Union cavalry under Pleasanton used by Union Commander General McClellan as skirmishers probing for the enemy throughout the day of fighting.

maps.name: Pry Grist Mill
maps.description: Skirmish map in the Antietam campaign.

maps.name: Pry House
maps.description: Skirmish map in the Antietam campaign.

maps.name: Railroad Cut
maps.description: Conquest map in the Drill Camp campaign.

maps.name: Reno's Fall
maps.description: September 14th - 18:00 close to Fox's Gap: After the Confederate collapse at Fox's Gap earlier in the day due to the attacks by Union Maj. Gen. Reno's IX Corps, CSA Brig. Gen. Hood now orders his division south to relieve the battered Confederate lines in an effort to regain a foothold at the gap. To deny the Confederates the chance of doing so, the 51st New York and Pennsylvania are sent forward with the Corps commander in close proximity in order to inspire his troops and inspect the lines.

maps.name: River Crossing
maps.description: September 15th - 09:30: In this fictitious scenario, Confederates under General McLaws desperately attempt to cross the Potomac River to assault the town of Harper's Ferry from both sides.

maps.name: River Town
maps.description: Conquest map in the Harpers Ferry campaign.

maps.name: Rocky Slopes
maps.description: Conquest map in the South Mountain campaign.

maps.name: Roulette Lane
maps.description: September 17th - 12:45: The 3rd Arkansas and 27th North Carolina under Colonel Cooke find themselves on the flank of the Federals now in possession of the Sunken Road. The 1st Delaware and 14th Indiana are tasked with holding the rebels back at Roulette Lane.

maps.name: School House Ridge
maps.description: September 15th - 06:30: During the siege of Harper's Ferry, General Stonewall Jackson had lined a large portion of his force along Schoolhouse Ridge, which sat opposite a valley overlooked by the Bolivar Heights, which the Union had hastily fortified. In this fictitious scenario, the Confederates attempt to make a frontal charge against the strong defenses of the Union!

maps.name: Shenandoah Street
maps.description: September 15th - 13:30: In this semi-fictitious scenario, AP Hill has broken past the southern defenses of Bolivar Heights, and is now threatening to take the downtown region of Harper's Ferry as blue-clad defenders scramble to stop the Confederates.

maps.name: Smith Field
maps.description: Whatever the soldier’s reasons for enlisting to fight the war, nothing concerned him more than his pay. Infrequent and meager compensation frequently left both Union and Confederate soldiers, and their dependents back home, in dire circumstances.

maps.name: Smokestacks
maps.description: Conquest map in the Antietam campaign.

maps.name: South Woodlot
maps.description: Union and Confederate soldiers widely despised sutlers, merchants who accompanied the army providing essential and luxury goods at exorbitant prices. Reliance on sutlers to supplement meager rations after a hard march led to the financial ruin of many soldiers.

maps.name: Stefan's Lot
maps.description: The unprecedented concentration and skillful deployment of artillery at the Battle of Antietam resulted in its grim moniker, "Artillery Hell." Both the soldiers who worked the guns and those who were put in their crosshairs could entirely relate.

maps.name: Towering Trunks
maps.description: Conquest map in the Drill Camp campaign.

maps.name: Union Camp
maps.description: Although many soldiers wrote of looking forward to experiencing battle - frequently described as “seeing the elephant” - they often discovered that combat beggared description and was nothing like the dime novels of their youth made it out to be.

maps.name: Valley
maps.description: Conquest map in the Harpers Ferry campaign.

maps.name: Wagon Road
maps.description: With the Second Great Awakening still fresh in the minds of many, religion played at least some role in the lives of the common soldier, especially when their regiment had the benefit of a chaplain.

maps.name: Washington Street
maps.description: September 15th - 15:30: In this fictitious scenario, the Union garrison attempt to defend against Confederates now streaming down Camp Hill by way of the main thoroughfare to Harper's Ferry from Bolivar - Washington Street.

maps.name: Waterways
maps.description: Conquest map in the Antietam campaign.

maps.name: West Woods
maps.description: September 17th - 10:00: General Edwin Sumner's Union Second Corps advances into the West Woods where they are met by Confederate Wing Commander Jackson's men. Union General John Sedgwick's division is performing a series of reckless charges into the Confederates at very high costs to break the Confederate line.

maps.name: Wheat Fields
maps.description: Conquest map in the South Mountain campaign.

maps.name: Antietam (Onslaught)
maps.description: Onslaught map in the Onslaught campaign.

maps.name: Drill Camp (Onslaught)
maps.description: Onslaught map in the Onslaught campaign.

maps.name: Harpers Ferry (Onslaught)
maps.description: Onslaught map in the Onslaught campaign.

maps.name: South Mountain (Onslaught)
maps.description: Onslaught map in the Onslaught campaign.
